claims.text: Cost information is the record of what it costs a business to make its products or run its operations, broken down so that it can be attached to particular products, departments or activities.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business needs cost information to set prices that cover what it spends, to decide which products and activities to continue, to control spending against a plan, and to judge how it is performing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Inaccurate cost information can mislead any decision that materially depends on the figure, and the direction of the error follows the direction of the distortion. A product charged with too little cost looks more profitable than it is, so it may be priced too low or pushed too hard; a product charged with too much looks like a failure, so it may be dropped although it was helping to cover costs that would be incurred anyway. Because a shared total divided between products is a fixed sum, understating one product's share normally overstates another's, so two products can be distorted in opposite directions at the same time. Whether a particular decision goes wrong depends on whether the error is large enough to change it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-12 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R3 (R3-001). The original said every decision resting on an inaccurate figure is wrong in the same direction. Neither half holds: an error need not be material to every dependent decision, and allocating a fixed shared total is zero-sum, so understating one product's share overstates another's - opposite directions, not a common one.

claims.text: Accuracy is hardest, and matters most, where costs are shared between products, because a shared cost has to be divided using a chosen method rather than simply measured.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A fixed cost does not change as output changes over a given period. Rent, insurance, business rates and the salaries of permanent staff are fixed costs: the business pays them whether it produces nothing or works at full capacity.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A variable cost changes directly with output. Raw materials, packaging, and wages paid per item produced are variable costs: produce nothing and they are nothing; double output and they roughly double.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A fixed cost is fixed only within a range of output and for a period of time. A business that outgrows its factory has to rent a second one, and the rent then steps up to a new level at which it is again fixed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Total cost = fixed costs + total variable costs, where total variable cost = variable cost per unit x output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: As output rises, fixed cost per unit falls, because the same total is spread over more units, while variable cost per unit stays the same. This is why producing more usually lowers the average cost of each unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can reduce its variable cost per unit by buying materials in larger quantities at a lower price, cutting waste in production, finding a cheaper supplier of the same quality, or redesigning the product to use less material.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A direct cost can be attributed in full to one product, department or activity. The leather in a shoe and the wages of the worker who makes only that shoe are direct costs of that shoe.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An indirect cost, also called an overhead, cannot be attributed to a single product without dividing it up. Factory rent, the finance department's salaries and the electricity for the whole site are indirect costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The fixed and variable split describes how a cost behaves as output changes. The direct and indirect split describes whether a cost can be traced to one product. They are separate questions, so a cost can be direct and fixed at the same time: the salary of a supervisor who works on one product line only.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Dividing an indirect cost between products requires a basis to be chosen - floor space, machine hours, labour hours, units produced. A different basis gives a different cost per product from the same real spending, so the product cost that results is a judgement rather than a measurement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because the basis is chosen, a product can be made to look profitable or unprofitable by the way overheads are shared out, which is a problem when the figure is then used to decide whether to keep making it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Full costing assigns every cost to the products: the direct costs of each product plus a share of the costs the business incurs as a whole, fixed overheads included.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. Aligned with the corrected boundary in CLM-032.

claims.text: Contribution costing assigns only the variable costs to products and treats fixed costs as a cost of the period, to be covered out of the combined contribution of everything the business sells. A variable cost shared between products still has to be divided before it can be charged to one of them, so the method reduces allocation rather than removing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. The original implied contribution costing never allocates anything, which is untrue of shared variable costs.

claims.text: The difference between the two methods is what each does with fixed costs. Full costing assigns all of a business's costs to its products - the direct costs of each product plus a share of everything else, including fixed overheads. Contribution costing assigns only the variable costs to products and treats fixed costs as a cost of the period. So a cost that is direct but fixed, such as a supervisor employed on one line only, is inside the full cost of that line and outside its contribution cost; and a variable cost that is shared, such as power used by several products, is in both, though it still has to be divided before either method can charge it to one product.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. The original said the methods differ over 'fixed and indirect' costs as though those were one category, and that direct and variable costs are treated alike. That contradicted this topic's own teaching that a cost can be direct and fixed. The boundary is fixed versus variable, not direct versus indirect.

claims.text: Full costing gives a cost per unit that covers everything the business spends, which makes it a sound basis for a long-run price, and it is straightforward where a business makes one product, because there is nothing to share out.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The limitation of full costing is the share-out. The basis is chosen rather than measured, a different basis changes each product's cost, and a product can appear to make a loss purely because of the size of the overhead share it was given. Where those overheads are unavoidable - a lease that runs on, staff the business keeps - stopping the product removes its contribution and leaves the costs to be carried by fewer products. Where some of them would genuinely disappear with the product, that part belongs in the decision and the recorded loss may be real.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. The original stated overhead continuation as certain. Only unavoidable common overhead remains.

claims.text: Contribution per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Total contribution = contribution per unit x number of units sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each unit sold contributes its selling price less its own variable cost towards the fixed costs of the business. Once the fixed costs are fully covered, every further unit's contribution becomes profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit = total contribution - fixed costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contribution is not profit. Contribution is what is left from a sale after the variable costs of making it; profit is what is left after the fixed costs of the period as well. A business can have a large total contribution and still make a loss if its fixed costs are larger.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A product whose selling price is above its variable cost makes a positive contribution. Dropping it without putting anything in its place loses that contribution while any fixed cost that would have been incurred anyway remains, so the business ends up worse off by the contribution lost less whatever cost genuinely disappears with the product. That is what positive contribution proves. It does not prove that keeping the product is the best available decision: that also depends on whether the capacity it uses could earn a larger contribution doing something else.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-12 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R3 (R3-002). The original concluded that a positive-contribution product is worth continuing where the fixed costs would be incurred anyway. Positive contribution establishes the loss from dropping WITHOUT replacement; it says nothing about whether the capacity could earn more in another use, which is the second condition of the keep decision.

claims.text: Contribution costing leaves fixed costs out of the product figure, so a business that sets prices on contribution alone can cover its variable costs on every sale and still not cover its fixed costs overall.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contribution costing assumes the variable cost per unit stays the same at every level of output, which is not always so: bulk buying can lower it, and overtime or a strained supply chain can raise it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Repeatedly accepting work priced above variable cost but below full cost can make it harder to charge the full price elsewhere, if customers learn that a lower price is available.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contribution costing suits a short-run decision in which the fixed costs will not change whatever is decided: whether to accept a one-off order with spare capacity, which of two products to push, or whether to stop making something.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contribution costing does not suit a decision that changes the fixed costs themselves, such as opening a second site, and it does not suit setting a long-run price, which has to cover everything the business spends.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Total cost is everything it costs to produce a given level of output: fixed costs plus total variable costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Average cost, or cost per unit, = total cost / output.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit. At AS level, where the variable cost per unit is treated as constant, the marginal cost of one more unit is its variable cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Average cost and marginal cost answer different questions. Average cost tells a business what each unit has cost on the whole; marginal cost tells it whether making one more unit adds more revenue than cost. A business with spare capacity can find that an extra unit is worth making even at a price below average cost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost-plus pricing sets the price by taking the cost per unit and adding a mark-up: price = cost per unit + (cost per unit x mark-up percentage).

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which cost a price is compared with depends on the question being asked. For a one-off order, the test is whether the price exceeds every cost the order itself causes - its variable cost plus any extra fixed cost it creates - and whether the capacity it uses would otherwise have earned more. Where it does, the order improves profit or reduces a loss, whatever the rest of the order book is doing. For the long run, the test is different: total contribution across everything sold has to cover the fixed costs at a volume the business can realistically achieve, so a price set above full cost per unit is only as good as the output figure that full cost was calculated at.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. The original made prior coverage of fixed costs a necessary condition for an order to add to profit, which is false - positive incremental contribution reduces a loss as readily as it adds to a profit. It also treated a price above full cost as guaranteeing profit, which holds only at the assumed volume.

claims.text: Setting a price from cost alone ignores what customers are willing to pay and what competitors charge, so it can leave money on the table for a product people value highly, or set a price the market will not accept.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Revenue = selling price per unit x number of units sold. Profit = revenue - total costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Comparing this period's cost per unit with the plan, with an earlier period, or between departments shows where spending is rising and narrows the search for a cause; the comparison is what makes the figure useful, not the figure on its own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cost information can only show where to look. Whether a rise in cost per unit is a problem depends on why it happened - a fall in output raises fixed cost per unit without anybody having spent more.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A special order is a one-off request to supply at a price below the normal one.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A special order is worth taking when the revenue it brings in exceeds every cost it actually causes - its variable cost, plus any setup, extra labour, delivery or other fixed cost incurred only because of this order - and when the capacity it uses would not otherwise have earned more. Where both hold, the order improves profit or reduces a loss. The fixed costs the business would pay anyway are not part of that comparison, but the ones the order creates are.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-12 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R2. The original reduced the test to price above variable cost plus spare capacity, which omits order-specific incremental costs and the opportunity cost of the capacity.

claims.text: A special order should be judged on more than the contribution it earns: whether existing customers will learn of the lower price, whether the capacity used would otherwise have gone to full-price work, and whether the buyer will expect the same price again.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis compares a business's revenue with its costs at different levels of output in order to find the level at which the two are equal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The break-even level of output is the number of units at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis matters because it converts a plan into a number a business can act on: the minimum it must sell to avoid a loss, how far sales can fall before it makes one, and what either of those figures becomes if the price, the costs or the volume change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even level of output = fixed costs / contribution per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: On a break-even chart, output is on the horizontal axis and money on the vertical. The total revenue line starts at the origin; the total cost line starts at the level of the fixed costs. They cross at the break-even level of output, and the gap between them to the right of that point is profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business can lower its break-even level of output in three ways, and each works through the formula: raise the selling price or cut the variable cost per unit, both of which raise contribution per unit, or cut the fixed costs themselves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The break-even formula can be rearranged for what a question actually asks. Fixed costs = break-even output x contribution per unit. The price needed to break even at a chosen volume = (fixed costs / that volume) + variable cost per unit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Margin of safety = current or budgeted output - break-even output. It is the amount by which sales can fall before the business stops making a profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The margin of safety can be given in units or as a percentage of current output. Expressed as a percentage it is easier to compare between businesses of different sizes and between periods.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit at a given level of output = (contribution per unit x units sold) - fixed costs. The same figure can be found as margin of safety x contribution per unit, because every unit sold beyond break-even adds its whole contribution to profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: At any output below break-even the business is making a loss equal to the fixed costs not yet covered; at break-even the profit is zero; above it, profit grows by the contribution per unit for every additional unit sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business uses break-even analysis to set a sales target, to test the effect of a price change or a cost increase before committing to it, to judge whether a new product or site is worth starting, and to support an application for finance by showing a lender what has to be sold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis rests on assumptions that simplify reality. It assumes everything produced is sold, that the selling price is the same at every volume, that the variable cost per unit does not change, and that every cost can be sorted cleanly into fixed or variable. Each assumption can fail, and the answer is only as good as they are.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Break-even analysis is also a snapshot built on forecast figures. It dates as soon as a cost or a price moves, and a chart drawn for a business selling several products assumes the mix between them stays the same.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The limitations set the weight break-even analysis can bear. It is at its most useful for isolating the arithmetic effect of changing one stated input while the others are held where they are, which is what makes it a sensitivity test. It is weakest as a prediction, because then the assumptions are the answer. Isolating an effect is not the same as proving an option better: the inputs held constant may themselves respond to the change - a price rise can move volume, a cheaper input can move quality - so the comparison has to be finished by asking which held-constant figures would not in fact hold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

notes: Repaired 2026-09-10 after review SR-9609-5.4-CODEX-R1. The original said the assumptions 'largely cancel out' when two options are compared. They do not: an assumption can be wrong in different directions under each option, which is exactly what this topic's own price-rise evaluation says.
